content: Improved treatment success rates have been linked to enhanced patient support, which includes assistance with medication adherence. This support can be provided through digital technologies or other methods as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Unlike the treatment regimens for drug-susceptible tuberculosis (TB) and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), the recommended treatment regimen for isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) does not include distinct intensive and continuation phases. This simplifies the delivery and monitoring of treatment. Studies included in the individual patient data (IPD) analysis utilized regimens containing levofloxacin (typically 750–1000 mg/day), moxifloxacin (400 mg/day), or gatifloxacin (400 mg/day). Early-generation fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, were also used but are no longer recommended for the treatment of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). For detailed information on dosing regimens, refer to the Frequently Asked Questions on the WHO Treatment Guidelines for Isoniazid-Resistant Tuberculosis, available on the same website as these guidelines. Patients receiving the (H)REZ-Lfx regimen require close monitoring during treatment through scheduled clinical and laboratory testing. The definitions used to assign treatment outcomes are consistent with those for drug-susceptible TB. Signs of non-response or treatment failure should prompt drug susceptibility testing (DST) for rifampicin and, if possible, for fluoroquinolones and pyrazinamide. To minimize the risk of acquiring additional resistance, adding single TB medicines should be avoided in patients who remain smearor culture-positive after two months of treatment, show no favorable clinical response, or lack recent DST results. Safety precautions are essential to rapidly identify and manage any serious adverse events (SAEs). Close clinical monitoring, particularly liver function tests, is crucial due to the hepatotoxic potential of prolonged pyrazinamide use. Monthly testing for aspartate aminotransferase (AST or SGOT) levels is recommended for all patients, if resources allow. If resources are limited, monthly monitoring should focus on high-risk patients, such as those co-infected with viral hepatitis or with a history of heavy alcohol use. In pediatric populations, adherence to correct dosing is critical to prevent ethambutol toxicity, which can be detected early in older children through red-green color discrimination tests. Monitoring for retrobulbar neuritis should also be conducted when appropriate. Although only 2% of Hr-TB patients in the IPD review were children, the results and recommendations can likely be extrapolated to pediatric patients, as the regimen components have been standard TB medicines for children for many years. For patients with extensive disease, extending the 6-month (H)REZ-Lfx regimen beyond six months may be considered on an individual basis, particularly for those with cavitary disease or persistent bacteriologically positive sputum at or after month three. However, treatment prolongation may increase the risk of adverse events. In HIV-positive individuals, the effect of longer TB treatment durations has been studied in drug-susceptible TB patients. Among HIV-infected patients not on antiretroviral therapy (ART), those receiving six months of treatment had a fourfold higher risk of poor outcomes compared to those with treatment extended to nine months. For HIV-positive TB patients, initiating ART within eight weeks of starting TB treatment is a priority, as per WHO guidelines. The 6-month (H)REZ-Lfx regimen is recommended for HIV-positive patients. No specific data were available for patients with exclusively extrapulmonary Hr-TB. However, the proposed regimen is likely effective in these cases. Treatment for extrapulmonary TB should be designed in consultation with specialists, such as infectious disease physicians and neurologists, to tailor treatment duration and supportive care as needed. Treatment with rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, with or without isoniazid, has been used in recent years for Hr-TB patients. Evidence reviews focused on whether treatment outcomes could be improved by adding a fluoroquinolone or streptomycin to (H)REZ regimens of varying durations. The IPD analysis, which included data from 33 databases and 5418 Hr-TB patients, informed recommendations for regimens containing these anti-TB agents. A six-month (H)REZ regimen demonstrated higher treatment success rates compared to regimens longer than six months. Further analyses showed no statistically significant difference in outcomes between six-month and longer regimens. However, reducing the duration of pyrazinamide use to three months or less was associated with worse outcomes, particularly in regimens without a fluoroquinolone. The addition of streptomycin did not significantly reduce mortality and was associated with increased SAEs. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized the importance of balancing benefits and harms, considering patient preferences, equity, and feasibility. A six-month (H)REZ regimen, particularly one without injectable agents, was deemed likely to improve health equity and patient outcomes. The regimen's cost-effectiveness and feasibility in most DR-TB treatment settings were highlighted, especially with the use of fully oral medicines. Rapid DST for isoniazid and rifampicin resistance at diagnosis was identified as the most cost-effective strategy for preventing deaths and acquired MDR-TB. The GDG acknowledged the limitations of the evidence, including the inability to control for all confounding factors and the lack of standardized adverse event reporting. Nonetheless, the group agreed on the beneficial effects of the Hr-TB regimen when used in accordance with policy recommendations. Further research is needed to refine treatment policies and optimize Hr-TB management. WHO will work with regional and country offices, technical agencies, and partners to disseminate and implement these recommendations effectively.
